01 Why it matters

The maps disagree.

Zoning, fire hazard, and permit records are kept by different agencies, updated on different schedules, and published through different portals. When two official sources disagree and nobody catches it, the cost tends to show up later: a redesign, a re-bid, another correction cycle, or a deposit that went hard on an assumption.

Never guess. When the evidence can't support a conclusion, your brief says UNKNOWN and tells you what would settle it.

A parcel line isn't proof of a legal lot.

City map parcels and assessor numbers don't establish legal-lot status. If that question matters, the brief flags it for review against recorded documents and the appropriate professional or agency.

Two maps, two answers.

When official sources disagree, you see both values, each with its source and date.

Not online isn't "no."

A record missing from an online portal is a gap to close, not proof it doesn't exist.

An honest UNKNOWN before you commit beats a confident answer that turns out wrong.

02 How PermitPulse works

Every finding labeled. Every label cited.

Your brief sorts what we found into three labels. Each one comes with its source, a link, and the date we retrieved it.

  • SUPPORTED

    The official record says it. You get the link and the date.

  • CONFLICT≠

    Official sources disagree. You see both, side by side. We don't pick a winner.

  • UNKNOWN

    The record can't answer it yet. We tell you which document, agency, or professional can.

  1. Source

    We pull the official record.

    City zoning and planning data, CAL FIRE fire hazard maps, and available permit records. Each capture keeps its retrieval date.

  2. Map

    We line the sources up on one parcel.

    Each source is compared against the same property, so agreement and disagreement are visible, not assumed.

  3. Brief

    Every finding gets a label and a citation.

    Conflicts and unknowns are listed first, so the uncertainty you need to resolve is the first thing you read.

  4. Next questions

    You know what to verify next.

    For each open item, the brief names the document, agency, or professional that could settle it, and the question to ask.

In each brief

See an example brief →
  • The parcel record as the City publishes it, with retrieval date
  • Zoning and planning designations, quoted from the official source
  • Fire hazard severity zone status from CAL FIRE's state and local responsibility area maps, checked separately
  • Permit history highlights from available online records
  • Conflicts and gaps, listed first
  • The next questions to ask, and who to ask

  1. 01

    CAPTURED

    The official parcel record was pulled directly from the City's map service and saved as received with retrieval evidence.

  2. 02

    PRESERVED

    Source evidence was preserved so later changes could be detected.

  3. 03

    REVIEWED

    The parcel boundary was normalized with pinned mapping tools and reviewed as part of the operator workflow.

  4. 04

    CHECKED

    The parcel was compared against official CAL FIRE fire hazard map sources using separate authority routes.

  5. 05

    FLAGGED

    Official map data isn't always clean. When malformed or conflicting source geometry prevents a defensible answer, the check stays UNKNOWN.

  6. 06

    HELD

    Where a required review step remained open, the result stayed marked not ready. Nothing was rounded up to a yes or no.
